name: Colorado

notes: Food for home consumption is exempt from the 2.9% state tax and from RTD's, the cultural facilities district's and regional transportation authorities' taxes; counties and cities tax it unless they have adopted the exemption, and home-rule cities set their own rules (Denver exempts it; Fort Collins taxes it at 2.25%), so the local rate on groceries here is each place's own from the Department of Revenue's table. Candy and soft drinks are taxed at the full rate, which is not counted here.

Cigarettes and other tobacco pay the 2.9% state rate, on top of excise taxes left out here: $2.24 a pack of cigarettes ($2.64 from July 1, 2027) and 56% of the list price on other tobacco (Proposition EE); some cities and counties add their own per-pack cigarette taxes (Aspen, Vail, Eagle, Pitkin and Summit counties and others; noted on their pages, not counted). Of the local taxes the state collects, only RTD's and the Scientific and Cultural Facilities District's apply to cigarettes; county, statutory city and other district taxes don't (Department of Revenue), so tobacco is counted at those rates. Home-rule cities set their own rule: 47 whose codes, rules or forms were read exempt cigarettes (Denver, Colorado Springs, Boulder, Pueblo and Arvada among them) and are counted without the city rate on tobacco; Aurora, Fort Collins, Lakewood, Littleton, Loveland, Thornton, Westminster and Mountain Village tax them; the ten not checked are taken to tax them at the full rate. Other tobacco, which counties and cities do tax, isn't separated.

Household supplies: diapers and incontinence products are exempt from the state tax and RTD, cultural facilities and regional transportation authority taxes; city and county taxes apply unless the city or county has adopted the exemption. This is not taken out here.

Personal care products: period products have been exempt from the state tax since January 1, 2023, and from RTD, cultural facilities and regional transportation authority taxes; city and county taxes apply unless adopted locally. This is not taken out here.
Barber and beauty services aren't taxed.
Laundry and dry cleaning aren't taxed.

Motor fuel on which the excise tax is paid is exempt from the state sales tax and the local taxes the Department collects; it pays 22 cents a gallon plus fees (a 6-cent road usage fee and smaller environmental fees, about 30 cents in all), left out here. Home-rule cities set their own rules, not checked here.
Repair labor isn't taxed when stated separately from parts.
Colorado has no sales tax holiday.
A 31-cent retail delivery fee on taxable deliveries (since July 1, 2026, as reported) and local lodging taxes (Denver's 10.75% lodger's tax among them) are not counted here.

On November 3, 2026 Coloradans approved Proposition 137 (part of the state sales tax on sporting goods, redirected to conservation; no rate change), 1,074,969 for and 1,060,289 against, and voters in the Front Range Passenger Rail District approved its 0.333% sales tax (food, gasoline and medical items exempt; 2026 Blue Book), 436,785 for and 338,342 against (Secretary of State, unofficial counts). The district tax is counted once the Department of Revenue lists it; the current rates are used here.
gaps: Local rates from the Department of Revenue's workbook for July to December 2026: 64 counties and 284 places. 18 places lie in more than one county with a different rate in each part; in each census tract such a place's rate is that of its part in the tract's county, counted for the share of the tract's store jobs located in the place. Where part of a place or county lies in a district (RTD, a regional transportation authority, a local improvement, metropolitan, fire protection or health services district) at a higher rate, the rate runs up to it as a range (17 places and most counties).

Home-rule cities (65, Denver, Aurora and Colorado Springs among them) collect their own tax and set their own rules; their rates are from the same workbook (Lone Tree's from the city, which cut it to 2.5% in December 2023). Their rates on groceries are from each city's own page or, where it doesn't say, the Department of Revenue's online rate lookup: 18 exempt groceries (Denver, Aurora, Colorado Springs, Pueblo and Lakewood among them), Fort Collins, Greeley, Northglenn, Timnath and Vail tax them at a lower rate, and the rest tax them in full (Mount Crested Butte's own page says it taxes all goods, though the state's lookup shows groceries exempt). Grocery tax rebates for lower-income households (Boulder, Fort Collins, Greeley, Longmont) aren't counted.

Cigarettes pay the state's 2.9% and, of the taxes the state collects for local governments, only RTD's and the Scientific and Cultural Facilities District's; county, statutory city and other district taxes don't apply to them (Department of Revenue), so tobacco is counted at those rates only (other tobacco, which counties and cities do tax, isn't separated). Home-rule cities set their own rule. 52 whose codes, rules or tax forms were read exempt cigarettes (Arvada, Avon, Black Hawk, Boulder, Breckenridge, Brighton, Broomfield, Castle Pines, Castle Rock, Centennial, Central City, Cherry Hills Village, Colorado Springs, Commerce City, Cortez, Dacono, Delta, Denver, Durango, Englewood, Federal Heights, Frisco, Glendale, Glenwood Springs, Golden, Grand Junction, Greeley, Greenwood Village, Lafayette, Lamar, Lone Tree, Longmont, Louisville, Montrose, Monument, Mount Crested Butte, Northglenn, Parker, Pueblo, Ridgway, Rifle, Sheridan, Silverthorne, Snowmass Village, Steamboat Springs, Telluride, Timnath, Vail, Wheat Ridge, Windsor, Winter Park, Woodland Park) and are counted without the city's rate on tobacco; Aurora (since December 2019), Fort Collins (since June 2022), Lakewood, Littleton, Thornton, Westminster, Mountain Village, Craig, Crested Butte, Evans, Gypsum and Sterling tax them under their codes, as does Loveland, whose code follows the state's base. Every home-rule city's rule was read.

Telluride's and Mountain Village's 2% excise taxes on restaurant and bar sales, on top of their sales tax, are counted in their restaurant rates (each town's own page); other towns' separate restaurant taxes weren't checked.
Private improvement fees in parts of Firestone, Johnstown, Lakeside, Monument replace part of the city's tax there; they are not in the workbook, so those areas are shown at the city's full rate.

10 workbook locations are unincorporated communities, not Census places (Bailey, Como, Drake, Gateway, Glen Haven, Jefferson, Lake George, Ohio, Prospect Valley, Whitewater); they set the top of their county's range.

Downtown development authorities and business improvement districts come from the Department of Local Affairs' 2025 property-tax map and Denver's and Colorado Springs' own layers; Aurora's (2025) and Loveland's downtown development authorities aren't on the state's map, and Englewood's and Wheat Ridge's urban renewal areas have no official map.

warn.text: Buena Vista draws many visitors (rafting, hot springs and the Collegiate Peaks), but it isn't flagged as a visitor economy: its seasonal homes (5.3%) and its 5 lodging places (1.8 per 1,000 residents) fall under the flag's cutoffs. Visitors' spending is part of its local sales, so its retention rates likely overstate how much of residents' own spending stays local.
Glendale may be flagged as a visitor economy only because of its business hotels along Colorado Boulevard (11 lodging places, 2.4 per 1,000 residents), so read that flag with care.
